newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish c.bank reserve rise may signal flat rates.
newsitem.headline: Polish c.bank reserve rise may signal flat rates.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland's decision to increase mandatory reserves for banks could be a signal that the bank was intent on keeping official interest rates flat in the near-term, analysts said on Tuesday.
They said the decision could mean that the central bank opted for the reserves rise in order to cool fast growing credit action instead of increasing interest rates.

"There are two paths, higher interest rates or increased mandatory reserves, and amid good fundamentals it's politically better to change reserves," said Radoslaw Radziszewski, deputy chief dealer at Pekao SA.
"(Official) interest rates should remain unchanged until the end of the first quarter," Radziszewski added.

Late on Monday the central bank surprised the market by increasing mandatory reserves on zloty call deposits by three points to 20 percent and on currency deposits by two points to four percent, effective from February 28.

The central bank last said it wanted to see January's broad money data before making a decision on whether to raise official interest rates, now at 25 and 22 percent, to slow fast growing lending to the non-financial sector.

Analysts said that although the local money market had no initial reaction to the reserves rise, deposit rates may jump by up to one point in the later stages of February as banks prepared to brace for the impact of the increase.

"I think that for some two week's banks will observe and calculate...but later market's liquidity may fall which would push up market rates 0.7-1.0 point," said Konrad Greszta, director of the treasury department at PKO BP, the state savings bank.
Analysts said the reserves rise would most likely cause the bank to increase credit rates as their costs grow, but that competition would likely keep deposit rates from falling.
They also said the reserves rise was a cheaper method for the central bank's to cool credit action while keeping a lid on market rates.

"The NBP had an alternative instrument in increasing the scope of open market operations...but this move shoves the cost of these operations on to banks," Krzysztof Pietraszkiewicz, a director at the Polish Banking Association, told Reuters.
The central bank pushed market rates up by about two points to 22 percent since mid-December by pulling up its NBP-bill yields and reverse repo rates.
Analysts said the Polish zloty could also get a small boost after the NBP's decision to double the reserve requirement on foreign currency call deposits as banks shed hard currencies.

"Banks may be cutting foreign currency exposure as the cost for financing foreign currency deposits increases, but the effect on the zloty is likely to be minimal as banks already have short currency positions," said one foreign dealer here.
